past_medical_history: Prior diagnosis of 'functional neurological disorder' at age 38 (resolved)

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Anxious affect. Normal language. Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28/30.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: No obvious ptosis at rest. On extended sustained upgaze, subtle right ptosis develops at 90 seconds. No diplopia at rest. Faint right eye adduction lag on sustained rightward gaze for >60 seconds. Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. Facial sensation intact. No facial weakness at rest.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout at rest. After sustained arm elevation (deltoids) for 60 seconds, patient rates effort as 8/10 on fatigue scale. No objective weakness drop on brief repeat testing. Neck flexion 5/5 at rest.
neurological_exam.additional: No respiratory distress. NIF -62 cmH2O (normal). No dysphagia reported but patient notes food 'sticks' occasionally. Voice quality normal at rest, no fatigable dysarthria elicited on 10-minute examination.

patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating speech difficulty and swallowing problems for 6 months, initially thought to be anxiety
patient.history_present_illness: A 44-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder, fibromyalgia, and a prior episode of functional neurological disorder (at age 38, presenting with non-epileptic events, resolved) was admitted for evaluation of fluctuating dysarthria and dysphagia over 6 months. She reports her speech becomes slurred after about 20-30 minutes of prolonged speaking, particularly during work video conferences. She has noted occasional difficulty swallowing solid foods and has started cutting her food into smaller pieces. She also noticed intermittent drooping of her right eyelid, though this is inconsistent and she could not reliably reproduce it during outpatient visits. Her symptoms are consistently worse later in the day and improve significantly after rest. She saw her primary care physician who attributed symptoms to anxiety-related hyperventilation and muscle tension. She was referred to a gastroenterologist for dysphagia who performed upper endoscopy showing only mild GERD without structural abnormality. She was then referred to speech language pathology who noted mildly impaired swallowing on modified barium swallow but no aspiration. Her neurologist thought the fluctuating nature and prior functional neurological disorder history could represent somatization and referred her for cognitive behavioral therapy. She completed 8 sessions of CBT without improvement. Her dysarthria is specifically fatigable — she can speak normally in the morning but becomes increasingly slurred as the day progresses. She denies sensory symptoms, limb weakness at rest, diplopia during normal activities (though she mentions occasional brief double vision when tired at the end of the day that she attributed to eye strain), and headache. Her anxiety disorder has been stable on sertraline. Anti-AChR and anti-MuSK antibodies were checked at an outside facility 3 months ago and returned negative, which was used to exclude MG. She was not tested with SFEMG at the outside facility.

findings.test: NCS bilateral upper and lower extremities
findings.significance: Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes; no evidence of peripheral neuropathy

specialized_test.impression: Normal repetitive nerve stimulation study. No decremental CMAP response ≥10% in any tested muscle group. Maximum decrement 7% (nasalis). Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes on NCS; no post-exercise facilitation. A normal RNS study does not exclude a disorder of neuromuscular transmission, as sensitivity is approximately 75-80%; single-fiber EMG is recommended for higher sensitivity
recommended_actions: Single-fiber EMG recommended for higher sensitivity

output.test_type: Single-Fiber EMG — Orbicularis Oculi (facial muscle, most sensitive for ocular/bulbar MG)

findings.significance: Markedly increased jitter — highly abnormal for facial SFEMG
Also increased jitter in limb muscle — generalized NMJ disorder

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG. Increased jitter in orbicularis oculi (MCD 52 µs; reference <38 µs for facial muscles) and extensor digitorum communis (MCD 41 µs; reference <34 µs). Blocking in both muscles. Findings indicate severely impaired neuromuscular junction transmission and are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

results.title: Seronegative myasthenia gravis: diagnosis, pathophysiology, and treatment
results.finding: Approximately 5-10% of generalized MG patients are seronegative for all three AChR antibody subtypes and MuSK; SFEMG sensitivity remains >95% in seronegative MG; normal RNS does NOT exclude MG

results.title: Anti-LRP4 antibodies in seronegative MG
results.finding: Anti-LRP4 positive in 1-5% of double-seronegative MG; testing recommended in all seronegative cases

results.title: Avoiding misdiagnosis of functional disorders in seronegative MG
results.finding: Seronegative MG is frequently misdiagnosed as functional neurological disorder or anxiety; average diagnostic delay 2.3 years; SFEMG should be pursued in any patient with clinical fatigable weakness regardless of serology

output.query: Myasthenia gravis misdiagnosis functional neurological disorder anxiety diagnostic delay

results.title: MG masquerading as functional disorder: a systematic review
results.finding: Seronegative MG with predominantly bulbar features is the most commonly misdiagnosed subtype; psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression) increases misdiagnosis risk by 3-fold; negative antibodies and normal initial EMG contribute to 28-month median diagnostic delay

results.title: Fatigability as the distinguishing feature of MG vs functional weakness
results.finding: True fatigability (objectively demonstrable decline in muscle contraction with repetitive testing) distinguishes MG from functional weakness; Hoover sign and collapsing weakness patterns absent in MG

output.proposed: Prednisone 20mg daily + azathioprine 50mg daily (titrating to 2-3 mg/kg/day) for seronegative MG in patient on sertraline and pregabalin
interactions: Azathioprine + allopurinol: MAJOR interaction — do NOT combine (xanthine oxidase inhibition causes azathioprine toxicity)
Prednisone + sertraline: mild CYP3A4 interaction; corticosteroids may reduce sertraline levels; monitor mood and anxiety
Azathioprine + sertraline: no significant pharmacokinetic interaction
contraindications: Check TPMT activity before azathioprine — TPMT-deficient patients at risk for life-threatening bone marrow suppression
Do NOT combine azathioprine with allopurinol (not currently prescribed but important to remember)
warnings: Monitor CBC monthly for first 3 months on azathioprine (myelosuppression risk)
Azathioprine onset of action 6-18 months — do NOT expect rapid response
Monitor anxiety symptoms on prednisone — corticosteroids can worsen anxiety and depression
alternatives: Mycophenolate mofetil 1g BID — alternative steroid-sparing; less monitoring burden than azathioprine

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Seronegative generalized myasthenia gravis (MGFA Class IIb), diagnosed by SFEMG after AChR/MuSK/LRP4 negative serology

differential.key_features: Prior FND label and anxiety background create anchoring risk; however, fatigable diurnal weakness with abnormal SFEMG jitter is incompatible with FND.
MuSK MG presents with bulbar predominance and poor RNS response; here MuSK negative but seronegative pool overlaps and clustered AChR assays should be considered.
LEMS shows baseline low CMAP and facilitation at 50 Hz; here SFEMG pattern is post-synaptic.
CMS typically presents in childhood; adult-onset seronegative cases warrant genetic panel if family history.
Background diagnosis does not explain fatigable ptosis, diplopia, or abnormal jitter.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 all negative (seronegative MG); TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No thymoma; thymic involution appropriate for age

optimal_actions.action: Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Clustered AChR cell-based assay may detect low-affinity antibodies missed by standard radioimmunoassay

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Order single-fiber EMG — the most sensitive test (>95%) and definitive in seronegative MG
Confirm AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 all negative on standard assays
Pursue clustered AChR cell-based assay if available
CT chest with contrast — thymoma screening still required even in seronegative MG
Therapeutic trial of pyridostigmine and document objective improvement (QMG/MG-ADL)
Document MG diagnosis to overturn the prior 'functional disorder' label in the chart
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT defer SFEMG on the grounds that 'antibodies are negative' or 'this is the patient's anxiety/FND background' — seronegative MG is well established and SFEMG is the gold-standard test.
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Seronegative status (AChR, MuSK, LRP4 negative) does NOT exclude MG — proceed to single-fiber EMG; clustered cell-based AChR assays detect additional cases.
A prior 'functional disorder' label is the dominant red herring here — diagnostic re-anchoring is required when objective signs (fatigability, abnormal SFEMG) emerge.
Negative AChR + negative MuSK + negative LRP4 still leaves clustered AChR cell-based assays and CMS genetic panels as next steps in younger patients.

red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of 'functional neurological disorder' at age 38; current GAD/fibromyalgia/IBS
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on functional/psychiatric etiology and stop the diagnostic workup before SFEMG.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior FND does not preclude later organic disease; objective fatigability, RNS findings, and SFEMG jitter are organic markers that override the anchoring bias.

red_herrings.data_point: Negative AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 serology
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude that MG is excluded and re-affirm functional diagnosis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: 10-15% of generalized MG is seronegative on conventional assays; SFEMG sensitivity is >95% and is the diagnostic test of choice here.
